::: {.lecture-video lecture="1"}
:::

*Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — [CS229](https://cs229.stanford.edu/), Stanford
University, Autumn 2018.*

The first lecture of CS229 does two things. It places the course among Stanford's
other machine-learning courses, and it draws, in about forty minutes at the board,
the map the remaining nineteen lectures fill in: learning from labelled examples,
learning to apply learning algorithms well, deep learning, learning from data with
no labels, and learning from reward. No algorithm is derived. What the lecture
supplies instead is the set of pictures — a scatter of house prices, a row of noughts
and crosses, two clouds of unlabelled points — that every later derivation is drawn
on top of, and it is worth having them clearly in mind before the mathematics
arrives.

## What the course assumes {#sec-assumes}

[10:22]{.t} The stated prerequisites are modest on paper: familiarity with basic
probability and statistics, basic linear algebra, and enough programming to write
non-trivial code. In 2018 the assignments moved from MATLAB and Octave to Python and
NumPy, which Ng presented as following the field rather than leading it.

The more useful guidance came from a question at [28:37]{.t} about how CS229
differs from CS229A and CS230. Ng's answer was not a list of topics but a statement
about depth. CS229A, taught as a flipped classroom built on his online course,
covers a similarly broad set of algorithms with much less mathematics; CS230 is
narrower, deep learning only, and also more applied. CS229 is the one that derives
things, and he was candid that the derivations make it a heavy course. His advice to
anyone unsure whether they were ready was to take CS229A first. He also pointed out
that the three overlap less than their titles suggest — students who took two at once
saw the same algorithms from different angles rather than the same lectures twice —
and closed with the remark that frames the rest of the course: AI is larger than
machine learning, and machine learning is larger than deep learning.

## Two definitions {#sec-definitions}

[36:17]{.t} Ng offers two definitions of machine learning, an informal one and an
operational one.

The informal one is usually credited to Arthur Samuel: machine learning is the field
of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly
programmed. That exact sentence does not appear in Samuel's paper, [Some Studies in
Machine Learning Using the Game of
Checkers](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.33.0210) (1959), and is better read as a later
paraphrase of it. Samuel's own wording describes programming a computer "to behave in
a way which, if done by human beings or animals, would be described as involving the
process of learning". The result the lecture attaches to it is in the paper, and it
is what made the work famous. Samuel's program, given the rules of checkers and a list
of board features with unknown weights, learned to play a better game than Samuel
himself, partly by playing against a copy of itself and keeping whichever set of
weights won. The abstract puts the training time at eight to ten hours of
machine-playing time.

Ng's point about this is historical. At the time the open question was whether a
computer could do anything it had not been explicitly told to do, and a program
that beat its own author was a direct answer. Today it is routine for a learning
algorithm to outperform people on a *narrow* task — a particular kind of speech
recognition, or Go given enormous amounts of computation and self-play — and he
stresses the word narrow. Samuel's checkers player was among the first cases of that
pattern.

The operational definition is Tom Mitchell's, from his 1997 textbook *Machine
Learning*, which calls something a *well-posed learning problem* when three things are
named. A program learns from experience $E$ with respect to a task $T$ and a
performance measure $P$ if its performance on $T$, as measured by $P$, improves with
$E$. [38:43]{.t} Applied to checkers, $T$ is playing the game, $E$ is the large
number of games the program plays against itself, and $P$ is the probability of
winning its next game against a new opponent. The value of the definition is that it
forces all three to be stated. A good deal of what goes wrong in applied machine
learning, which the course returns to in its lectures on strategy, is a project where
one of them was never pinned down: the team is measuring a $P$ that does not track
the $T$ they care about, or gathering an $E$ that does not resemble the situations the
system will face.

## Supervised learning: regression {#sec-regression}

[40:12]{.t} The most widely used kind of machine learning, and the subject of the
first third of the course, is supervised learning. Ng introduces it with the example
the next lecture formalises. Plot the size of each house in a dataset on the
horizontal axis and its sale price on the vertical, call the first $x$ and the second
$y$, and ask for the relationship between them. If you own a house of 1,250 square
feet and want to know what to ask for it, one answer is to fit a straight line to the
data and read the price off the line above 1,250.

![House size against price, with a straight line and a quadratic each fitted to the
same points by least squares, and the price each predicts for a 1,250 ft² house. The
data are synthetic, drawn to resemble the board sketch. *Computed by
`figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py`.*](../figures/01-introduction/diagram_regression.svg){#fig-regression}

That is the whole shape of supervised learning. You are given a training set of
inputs $x$ paired with the correct outputs $y$, and the job is to learn a mapping from
$x$ to $y$ good enough to apply to an $x$ you have not seen. The problem is called
*regression* when $y$ is continuous. Prices are rounded to the cent and so are not
literally real numbers, Ng notes, but nobody prices a house at $\pi$ million dollars
and for every practical purpose they are continuous.

A straight line is close to the simplest learning algorithm there is, and
@fig-regression shows why it is not the only candidate. A quadratic follows the
flattening of prices at the top end and has lower error on the training points
(an RMSE of 25.4 against 29.6 on this data). That comparison cannot settle the
question, though. A quadratic can never fit its training data worse than a line,
because every line is a quadratic whose $x^2$ coefficient is zero, and this
particular quadratic peaks at about 2,400 square feet and predicts that every house
larger than that is worth less. How to choose between models — the line, the
quadratic, or something richer, whether by hand or automatically — is one of the
questions Ng flags as recurring all quarter. It becomes the bias–variance discussion
of lecture 8.

## Supervised learning: classification {#sec-classification}

[43:04]{.t} The second example comes from a medical problem some of Ng's
collaborators worked on: deciding from a breast tumour's size whether it is malignant
or benign. Plot size on the horizontal axis and, on the vertical, $y = 1$ for malignant
and $y = 0$ for benign. When a new patient arrives with a tumour of a given size, the
learning algorithm should say how likely it is to be malignant. Because $y$ now takes
one of a small number of discrete values, this is *classification*. With two values
it is binary classification, and with, say, five types of cancer it is still
classification, just with five classes.

[45:37]{.t} Ng then redraws the same data in a form the course uses from then on.
Every example is pushed up onto a single horizontal line, and the label is carried by
the symbol rather than by the height: a nought for a negative example ($y = 0$), a
cross for a positive one ($y = 1$). Nothing is lost — @fig-tumour-1d shows both views
of identical data — but the second frees the vertical axis to hold a second
input.

![The tumour problem twice. Above, size against the label plotted as a height;
below, the same examples on one axis with the label carried by the symbol. Synthetic
data. *Computed by
`figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py`.*](../figures/01-introduction/diagram_tumour_1d.svg){#fig-tumour-1d}

[47:07]{.t} That is the step he takes next. Real problems rarely give you one number
to predict another; with the patient's age as a second feature, $x$ becomes a
two-dimensional vector of tumour size and age, and each example becomes a nought or
a cross in the plane. The task is now to separate the two kinds of mark, and the
algorithm the course reaches for first draws a straight line between them. That
algorithm is logistic regression, taken up in lecture 3, and it is what fitted the
boundary in @fig-tumour-2d.

![Two features, tumour size and patient age. The line is the decision boundary
logistic regression fits to these points by Newton's method; one malignant example
falls on the benign side of it. Synthetic data. *Computed by
`figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py`.*](../figures/01-introduction/diagram_tumour_2d.svg){#fig-tumour-2d}

## More features than you can draw {#sec-features}

[48:41]{.t} The two-feature picture is a teaching device. The group Ng describes used
many more measurements of each tumour: clump thickness, uniformity of cell size,
uniformity of cell shape, marginal adhesion. Those are attributes of the Wisconsin
breast cancer data ([Breast Cancer Wisconsin
(Original)](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/15/breast+cancer+wisconsin+original)),
which scores each of nine cytological features on a scale of one to ten. Nine
dimensions cannot be plotted. The algorithms of the coming weeks are therefore
written for an input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of any length, and the board
pictures are the $n = 2$ case drawn to build intuition.

[50:11]{.t} Ng then makes the remark of the lecture that most deserves a second
look. The support vector machine, he says, can represent each patient not by two
numbers or a million, but by an *infinite* list of features. His question is the one a
reader should ask: a computer cannot store infinitely many numbers, so how can that
work?

The answer, which lecture 7 develops, is that the algorithm never needs the features
themselves. It only ever needs inner products between pairs of feature vectors, and
for well-chosen feature maps that inner product has a closed form. A one-dimensional
example shows it. Map a scalar $x$ to the infinite vector

$$
\phi(x) = e^{-x^2/2}\left(1,\; x,\; \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{2!}},\; \frac{x^3}{\sqrt{3!}},\; \dots\right).
$$ {#eq-gaussian-features}

The inner product of two such vectors is a power series that sums exactly:

$$
\phi(x)^\top \phi(z) = e^{-x^2/2}\, e^{-z^2/2} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(xz)^k}{k!}
= e^{-x^2/2 - z^2/2 + xz} = e^{-(x-z)^2/2}.
$$ {#eq-gaussian-kernel}

The left-hand side is an inner product in infinitely many dimensions; the right-hand
side is one subtraction and one exponential. The generator for this chapter checks the
identity numerically. For $x = 0.7$ and $z = -0.4$, the first five coordinates of
$\phi$ already match the exact value $e^{-(1.1)^2/2} \approx 0.5461$ to within
$10^{-5}$, and ten match it to about $10^{-12}$. A function like the right-hand side of
@eq-gaussian-kernel is called a *kernel*, and this one is the Gaussian kernel. The SVM
is written so that features appear only inside such inner products, and that is the
whole of the trick Ng is foreshadowing.

## Learning to steer: ALVINN {#sec-alvinn}

[52:05]{.t} The idea underneath all of this, Ng says, is that during training the
algorithm sees inputs $x$ together with their labels $y$, and its job is to find a
mapping that produces the right $y$ for a new $x$. To show how far that idea goes, he
plays an old video of Dean Pomerleau's
[ALVINN](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1988/hash/812b4ba287f5ee0bc9d43bbf5bbe87fb-Abstract.html)
at Carnegie Mellon, a neural network that learned to steer a vehicle.

The set-up is supervised learning with a human as the labeller. While a person drives,
the vehicle repeatedly digitises the camera image of the road ahead, downsampled to a
small greyscale picture, and records the steering direction the driver chose at that
moment. The image is $x$ and the driver's steering is $y$. On screen the label is a
bright blob on a bar, a little left of centre when the driver is turning slightly left,
and the network's output is drawn on a second bar beneath it. At the start of training
the network's output is a grey smear across the whole bar, its way of saying it has no
idea which way to steer. As training proceeds the smear contracts to a sharp blob that
tracks the driver's. Then the driver takes their hands off the wheel and the network
steers. A later version in the video trains separate networks for one-lane and
two-lane roads, with an arbitrator choosing between them, and switches from one to the
other as the road changes.

Ng is clear that this is not how self-driving cars are built now. The example is in
the lecture because it is a supervised learning problem whose labels cost nothing
except someone driving, and because the techniques that make it work — gradient
descent and backpropagation — are the ones the course teaches in its first weeks and
in lectures 10 and 11.

## Machine learning strategy {#sec-strategy}

[58:01]{.t} The second area of the course, which the class notes file under learning
theory, is what Ng calls machine learning strategy, and his motivation for it is drawn
from practice rather than from theory. Visiting machine-learning teams at large
technology companies, he finds an enormous difference in how effectively two teams
apply *the same* algorithm. The failure he describes is a team that has spent six
months on an approach, where a look at the data shows that it was never going to work,
and that could have been seen at the start.

The decisions behind that are the everyday ones: whether to collect more data and
which data, whether to try a different algorithm, whether to rent faster GPUs and
train for longer, which architecture to use. [1:01:08]{.t} A learning algorithm,
he says, almost never works the first time, so what separates teams is how they debug.
His two analogies are both about debugging by principle rather than by reflex. One is a
friend who dealt with compiler errors by deleting every line that had one. The other is
the difference between an inexperienced engineer who starts optimising code at once and
an experienced one who runs a profiler first and changes only the bottleneck. The aim is
to turn what has been "black magic", tribal knowledge held by people with decades of
experience, into an engineering discipline that can be taught. That material comes in
lecture 8, the learning-theory discussion section, and lecture 12 on debugging and
error analysis.

Deep learning is the third area. Ng describes it as the part of the field moving
fastest and treats it as one tool among many. CS229 covers enough to train a neural
network from scratch in lectures 10 and 11, and leaves the depth to CS230.

## Unsupervised learning {#sec-unsupervised}

[1:04:57]{.t} Ng introduces unsupervised learning by redrawing the classification
picture and deleting the labels. You are given only the inputs $x$, no $y$, and asked
to find interesting structure in them. In the data on the board the structure is
visible at a glance — two clusters — and an algorithm the course covers, k-means
clustering, finds it. @fig-clusters runs that algorithm on synthetic points like the
board's. Starting from two arbitrary points as centres, it reaches a stable split in
three rounds of reassignment.

![Unsupervised learning on the same kind of picture as @fig-tumour-2d, but without
labels. Left, all the algorithm receives; right, the two groups k-means assigns, with
each group's centre marked. Synthetic data. *Computed by
`figures/01-introduction/make_diagrams.py`.*](../figures/01-introduction/diagram_clusters.svg){#fig-clusters}

The applications Ng lists show how much of clustering is grouping things that nobody
has named. Google News gathers thousands of articles a day by different reporters
into a single story, such as the BP oil-well spill. Genetic microarray data group
individuals by shared characteristics. Clustering groups machines in a data centre by
related workloads, finds the cohesive communities in a social network, and splits a
customer database into market segments that can be addressed separately. A colleague
of his has used it to group galaxies in astronomical data.

[1:08:12]{.t} A student asked the natural question: is unsupervised learning just
clustering? It is not. Unsupervised learning means any use of unlabelled data to find
something interesting, and clustering is one instance. Ng's second example is the
*cocktail party problem*. Put several microphones in a room where several people are
talking at once. Each microphone records an overlapping mixture of every voice, and
the task is to recover each speaker's voice cleanly. Nothing labels which sound came
from whom, which is what makes the problem unsupervised. The algorithm that solves it,
independent component analysis, is in lectures 15 and 16 and is a programming
exercise later in the course. His third example is text. From unlabelled text alone, word
representations can be learned that capture analogies such as *man is to woman as king
is to queen* and *Tokyo is to Japan as Washington, D.C. is to the United States*, the
result popularised by [Mikolov et al.
(2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781).

He also offered a judgement on the economics. Most of the value machine learning was
creating in 2018 came from supervised learning, while unsupervised learning had
important uses and was where much of the research frontier lay.

## Reinforcement learning {#sec-rl}

[1:11:19]{.t} The fifth area starts from a problem that defeats supervised learning:
if you were handed the keys to Stanford's autonomous helicopter, how would you write
a program to fly it? The difficulty is that *nobody knows* the optimal way to move a
helicopter's two control sticks, so there is no $y$ to label each state with, and no
expert whose every action is worth imitating as ALVINN imitated its driver.

[1:12:18]{.t} Ng's analogy is training a dog. You cannot show a dog the optimal way
to behave either. You let it do what it wants and say "good dog" when it does
something you like and "bad dog" when it does not, and over time it does more of the
first and less of the second. Reinforcement learning replaces the label with that
signal, called the *reward*. The helicopter flies however it likes, gets "good
helicopter" for an accurate manoeuvre and "bad helicopter" when it crashes, and the
algorithm's job is to find a way of acting that collects more reward over time. The
helicopter in the video is the Stanford autonomous helicopter, whose aerobatic flight
is described in [Abbeel et al.,
2006](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2006/hash/98c39996bf1543e974747a2549b3107c-Abstract.html)),
and a second clip applies the same reward-driven learning to a legged robot dog
learning to climb over obstacles.

The best-known successes of reinforcement learning were in games, Atari and AlphaGo.
Ng said he was as excited, or more, by its growing traction in robotics and in
optimising logistics systems. The course's last five lectures build it up from Markov
decision processes.

## The map of the course {#sec-map}

[1:11:11]{.t} Ng closes the overview with the list of the five areas. They map onto
this book as follows.

| Area | What it is about | Lectures |
| :--- | :--------------- | :------- |
| Supervised learning | learning a mapping from labelled pairs $(x, y)$ | 2–7, 9 |
| Learning theory and strategy | why learning works, and how to make it work in practice | 8, learning theory, 12 |
| Deep learning | training neural networks | 10–11 |
| Unsupervised learning | finding structure in $x$ alone | 13–16 |
| Reinforcement learning | learning to act from a reward signal | 16–20 |

: The five areas of CS229 and the lectures that cover them. {#tbl-map}

The order is deliberate. Supervised learning comes first because it is where both the
mathematics and the economic value are most developed, and every later area borrows
its notation. The next chapter starts there, with the house-price scatter of
@fig-regression and the first algorithm for fitting it.
